name: Đại Việt
summary: The Vietnamese state from independence in the 10th century to 1804. It defeated Mongol invasions three times and expanded south at the expense of Champa.

location.value: Northern and later central and southern Vietnam, ruled mainly from Thăng Long (Hanoi).

terrain.value: The Red River delta, mountains, and a long coast.
terrain.source: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

climate.source: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

resources.value: Wet rice, forest products, and the sea.
resources.source: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

disasters.value: Red River floods; dykes were built to control them.
disasters.source: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

population.value: About 1.2 million (1200), 1.6 million (1400) and 5.6 million (1539) (Wikipedia infobox).

urbanisation.value: Thăng Long became the capital in 1010.

disease.source: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

migration.value: Southward expansion (Nam tiến) settled Vietnamese in former Cham and Khmer lands.
migration.source: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

economicBase.value: Wet-rice farming with large dyke systems.
economicBase.source: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

tradeRoutes.value: Trade with China and Southeast Asia; Hội An was a later port.
tradeRoutes.source: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.
wealth.source: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

moneyAndTax.value: The Vietnamese văn coin, and briefly banknotes.

inequality.value: Royal family, mandarins, landowners and peasants.
inequality.source: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

governmentType.value: Absolute monarchy; from 1533 to 1788 the Lê emperors were ceremonial under military lords (Trịnh and Nguyễn).

keyRulers.value: Đinh Bộ Lĩnh (968), Lý Thái Tổ, Trần Hưng Đạo (general), Lê Lợi (1428), Lê Thánh Tông, Gia Long (last).

succession.value: Hereditary dynasties: Đinh, Lê, Lý, Trần, Hồ, Later Lê, Mạc, Tây Sơn.
succession.source: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

institutions.value: Confucian civil service exams; the Hồng Đức law code (1483).
institutions.source: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

stability.value: Long civil wars: Lê–Mạc, Trịnh–Nguyễn (1558–1775) and the Tây Sơn rebellion.

eliteConflict.value: The Trịnh and Nguyễn lords divided the country for two centuries.

armyAndTech.value: Infantry, war elephants, and river fleets; firearms from the 15th century.
armyAndTech.source: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

majorWars.value: Defeated the Mongol–Yuan invasions (1258, 1285, 1288); Ming occupation (1407–1427).
majorWars.source: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

territoryChange.value: Annexed Champa’s lands (decisive war in 1471) and later the Mekong delta.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: China (Song, Yuan, Ming), Champa, the Khmer, Siam.
alliancesRivals.source: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

inventions.source: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

scienceEducation.value: The Temple of Literature (1070) and the Imperial Academy (1076).
scienceEducation.source: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

openness.value: Adopted Chinese administration while defending independence.
openness.source: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

religion.value: Mahayana Buddhism (state religion early on), Confucianism, Taoism and folk religion.

languageWriting.value: Literary Chinese for government; Vietnamese in Chữ Nôm script.

artsArchitecture.value: The Temple of Literature and One Pillar Pagoda in Hanoi.
artsArchitecture.source: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

socialStructure.source: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

sharedIdentity.value: Resistance to Chinese rule, celebrated in heroes such as Trần Hưng Đạo and Lê Lợi.
sharedIdentity.source: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

ideasReligions.source: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

colonisation.value: Slowly annexed Champa and Cambodian lands.

riseSignals.value: Independence from China and unification by Đinh Bộ Lĩnh.

peakPeriod.source: Taylor, A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

outcome.value: Reunited by the Nguyễn; renamed Việt Nam in 1804.

sources.value: Vietnamese chronicles. Checked against Wikipedia (“Đại Việt”).

knownFor.label: Victory over the Mongols
knownFor.note: Trần Hưng Đạo used stakes in the Bạch Đằng river to wreck the Yuan fleet.

knownFor.label: Áo giao lĩnh robe
knownFor.note: Traditional cross-collared robes worn before the later áo dài.
